articles.title: Digital records curation practices in Institutional Repositories (IRs) at selected public universities in Kenya
articles.abstract: Institutional repositories (IRs) across universities receive, preserve and provide access to digital information assets and are expected to implement digital records curation approaches. This study aimed to assess the status of digital curation at IRs in selected public universities in Kenya. The Open Archival Information System (OAIS) Reference Model was used to investigate the problem. The study adopted a qualitative approach where data was collected through telephone interviews with university librarians and staff in charge of the IRs. Analysis of the data was done thematically and presented in narrative descriptions. Findings of the study showed that the selected public universities had established IRs that ingested digital records into their custody. The study further established that pre-ingest and post-ingest practices in the IRs did not meet the required standards. The study concluded that an elaborate study with a bigger sample size is required so as to corroborate the findings. The study recommended use of the OAIS Reference Model by IRs in the public universities to preserve, manage and provide access to digital records. Subsequently, this study lays the foundation for similar studies to be replicated on a larger magnitude, while contributing to the existing body of knowledge on digital records curation.

articles.title: How agreeing with or confronting canon can help us face the challenges of the information age?
articles.abstract: This paper is a reflection on the interview with Natasha Khramtsovsky, who presented her view of Jenkinson’s Canon. Sir Hilary Jenkinson’s works are little-known in Russia, but it does not mean that they are irrelevant to Russian archivists. In the time of digital transformation, the well-built traditional canon becomes an obstacle for the development of new practices. The best way to confront the canon is to identify, critically assess and rethink all its practical approaches as theoretical principles. In that sense, some of Jenkinson’s ideas become very valuable and can help us answer the challenges of the information age.

articles.title: An archive for a school for autistic learners: documenting a distinctive pedagogy
articles.abstract: This paper discusses the recently created Western Autistic School’s (WAS) archive. WAS is a school for early primary autistic learners, which aims to equip them with the skills they need to move into mainstream schools. To this end, WAS has developed a distinctive individual-focused teaching model for autistic learners over its four decades history, informed by academic theory and research, as well as practical trial and error. The first part of the paper outlines the nature of autism and provides a brief history of the school and the evolution of its pedagogy. The second part of the paper summarizes the content and aims of the archive, which is meant to function both as an historical record and an inclusive pedagogical resource, shaped by the voice of the autistic community.

articles.title: Toward understanding: practices as common ground and starting point reflections on perspectives from Russia: an interview with Natasha Khramtsovsky
articles.abstract: Cross-border understanding is the type of understanding that empowers seamless and authentic communication, where ideas being received are ideas being conveyed. It enables national archivists to comprehend international archives – not only what people do, but also what people care about and why. Such understanding has been a rare encountering in our professional lives despite that writings exist and contextualization has always been mandatory. Arriving at such understanding requires more than language fluency, explanation availability, and communication sophistication, the requirements that we all acknowledge and we all strive to satisfy. Obtaining cross-border understanding necessitates a genuine evoking of the sense that ‘if I were you’ and the means of infinite approximation, both physical and virtual, which may eventually bring out the state that ‘I see myself being you’. It will not be easy, in both the regards of consensus and resources, yet it will also be difficult to argue to ditch the idea without even trying. With the will, we can start with identifying common grounds, for example, managerial means and digital preservation concerns, forging cross-border understandings about them, using the understanding as a reliable base, and moving together to next bases. These reliable bases then become the metacontext against which future understandings can come along and flow around. In time, we – the international archival community – may arrive at a place where we can be naturally and habitually frank about what unites us and what distinguishes us. A tall order indeed but one that warms our heart and helps our mission.

articles.title: The evolution of archival policies and regulations in China: a topic modelling approach
articles.abstract: This study investigates the development of China’s archival policies and regulations from 1949 to 2023, tracing the evolution of key topics. By employing Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) topic modelling, a comprehensive analysis was performed on 1,432 legal rules and regulations. The findings reveal four overall topics that have shaped China’s archival policies and regulations: Administrative Management, Scientific and Technological Archives Management, Services and Utilization, and Archives Management and Preservation. Additionally, this research identifies five distinct stages in the development of China’s archival policies and regulations, examining the changes in these topics across each stage. The contribution of this study lies in its semantic analysis of archival policies and regulations over a significant timeframe, highlighting crucial aspects of China’s archival policies and regulations and their evolution in response to socio-political and technological shifts. Ultimately, it provides a comprehensive overview of China’s archival policy and regulatory landscape.

articles.title: Records of resilience: preserving and promoting de-identified access to the Whitechapel Clinic records
articles.abstract: Many archive services, particularly those holding healthcare records, impose time-limited restrictions on access to records containing personal data, whilst allowing some limited ethical research access to these records. Access requests are considered in line with the current legislation and archive sector guidance, but it can be unclear to decision-makers which aspects of the complex legislative and regulatory environment relating to health and social care research in the UK pertain to archival access requests. This paper focuses on a case study of the archives of the Whitechapel Clinic, held by Barts Health NHS Trust Archives. It outlines the administrative history of the clinic and the custodial history of its records. It then examines how a request for research access to the records in 2011 led to an innovative collaboration between historians and archivists which supported long-term preservation of the archival data and generated a digital resource designed to satisfy privacy, confidentiality, and NHS research ethics requirements, which has since stimulated significant research. The authors conclude by suggesting a list of points for consideration by researchers proposing to access similarly sensitive and/or restricted records. They endorse recent calls for a collaborative review of current processes and guidance regarding access to restricted records.
